Need to search first.I've put together notes for all 17 verses, but the coverage is uneven. My search tool hit its usage limit partway through, so I could only use a few sources:

- Spurgeon's *Treasury of David*, which also quotes Calvin, Plumer, Fausset and Diodati
- Guzik on enduringword.com
- Gill, Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary and Matthew Henry (biblehub.com, blueletterbible.org)
- Barnes and Coffman (studylight.org)
- Utley on bible.org

Nothing came back from Lutheran, Methodist, Pentecostal, Catholic or Orthodox sites, netbible.org, or any prosperity or word-of-faith teaching. I couldn't read Augustine either. Section 2 (where Protestant traditions differ) is therefore almost empty, and section 3 has only the scholarly debate about when the psalm was written. I did find a few non-Protestant views, but only where other commentators mention them.

---

## Psalm 59 – Notes

**Title / setting**
- Gill: the occasion is 1 Samuel 19:11, when Saul's men watched David's house to kill him in the morning. He adds that the Syriac version's heading reads the psalm as being about Gentiles coming to faith and Jews being rejected. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/59.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: Michal warned David, and he escaped through a window during the night. It accepts the title as David's because it carries more weight than critics' guesses, which disagree with one another. It divides the psalm into four stanzas (vv. 1–5, 6–9, 10–13, 14–17). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-59.html
- Spurgeon: the music of worship owes a lot to the saints' trials. If Saul had never hunted David, the church would not have this song. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps059.php
- *Other view (scholars):* Ellicott says Ewald linked the psalm to a Scythian invasion under Josiah, a theory Ellicott finds "fascinating" but hard to give up. The "dogs" and the "heathen" could point to foreign raiders, but the focus on the enemies' words suggests slander rather than military attack. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/59.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary lists critics who think the speaker is the nation (De Wette), a late king of Judah (Ewald), a Maccabean leader (Hitzig) or a poet from Nehemiah's time (Koster). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-59.html
- Utley thinks the enemies look like foreign invaders, possibly with help from inside, and that "me" stands for a leader of Israel. On this view, an attack on him is an attack on the covenant people. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21558

**v. 1**
- Guzik: the man after God's own heart had many enemies, which is less surprising when we remember how many enemies the Son of David had. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-59/
- Guzik and Ellicott both say "defend/protect" literally means "set me on high," as if lifted into a safe high place. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-59/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/59.htm
- A note quoted by Spurgeon says David has two arguments: God is *his* God (the covenant), and his enemies are strong. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps059.cfm
- Gill reads the verse at three levels: David, Christ (whose enemies were the chief priests and Pharisees), and the church (whose enemies are sin, Satan and the world). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/59.htm
- Matthew Henry similarly hears the voice of David, of Christ, of the church and of the believer. He applies the verse to daily prayer against temptation and our own corrupt hearts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/59-1.htm
- A commentator on the same biblehub page says David means Saul but speaks in the plural out of respect for his king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/59-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: the plot came from the top of government, and some hoped to win Saul's favour by killing David. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-59/
- Gill: piling up requests in vv. 1–2 shows how desperate and earnest David was. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/59.htm
- Pulpit: foreign enemies are never called "bloody men," because fighting is their trade. That suggests these are enemies at home. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/59.htm

**v. 3**
- Barnes: "lie in wait" is ambush language, like a wild beast ready to spring, and "soul" here means "life." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-59.html
- Spurgeon: while the enemy crouches like a beast, we wait before God in prayer. Calling David's only "fault" too much courage and grace, he says the envious king couldn't rest. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps059.php
- Guzik: David isn't claiming to be sinless, only that Saul had no just reason. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-59/
- Pulpit: protesting complete innocence is typical of David's early psalms. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/59.htm
- Gill: one of the words means "rebellion," and David had committed no treason. Gill applies the verse to Christ, who was entirely without sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/59.htm

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: "run and prepare" may both be military terms. The word for "help me" literally means "meet" and is otherwise used in a hostile sense. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/59.htm
- Barnes and Utley read "help me" as a prayer that God would come to meet him. Utley links it to v. 10. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-59.html ; https://bible.org/book/export/html/21558
- Plumer (quoted by Spurgeon and Guzik): the zeal of the wicked should shame the slackness of the saints. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps059.cfm
- Spurgeon: "awake" means "when others sleep, keep watch, O God." https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps059.php
- Gill: God never sleeps but can seem asleep when he holds back. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/59.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik, quoting Maclaren: each of the piled-up names of God gives a reason to hope. David's own case makes him think of God putting things right worldwide. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-59/
- Matthew Henry: Saul has armies, so David appeals to the Lord of all armies. His enemies are strangers at heart, so he appeals to the God of Israel. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_059.cfm
- Ellicott: "the nations" (foreign foes) and "wicked traitors" (disloyal Israelites working with them) are contrasted, and the Hebrew phrase suggests hiding and treachery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/59.htm
- Pulpit: "all" includes wicked Israelites. Saul's agents included real foreigners, such as Doeg the Edomite, and godless Israelites. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/59.htm
- On "show no mercy," Spurgeon says to be merciful to them as people but not as transgressors, and not to overlook oppression. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/59-5.htm
- Gill: God is merciful to sinners but not to persistent, treacherous apostates. He says the alternative would seem to go against Christ's command. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/59.htm
- Gill also suggests "visit the nations" could mean visiting them with grace, through the gospel going to the Gentiles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/59.htm
- The Geneva note asks God to punish the reprobate who persecute his church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/59-5.htm

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: the half-wild dogs of Eastern cities sleep by day and roam in packs at night. The watchers came back each evening and either roamed about or guarded the gates so David couldn't escape. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/59.htm
- Ellicott: the verbs are better read as futures, and "howl" fits. He quotes a traveller describing Constantinople's 60,000 dogs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/59.htm
- Gill links the verse to Judas going out at night, and says "they shall return" can also be read prophetically of the final judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/59.htm

**v. 7**
- Barnes: "spew" means words gushing out like a spring. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-59.html
- Spurgeon: "they speak daggers." "Who can hear?" shows they feared neither God nor government, and David could probably hear their foul talk from the house. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps059.php
- Guzik: David may literally have heard them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-59/
- Ellicott suggests a small change to the Hebrew: "Spears they pour out with their mouths." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/59.htm
- Matthew Henry: people who think God doesn't notice what they say won't care what they say either. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/59-1.htm

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: compare Psalm 2:4. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/59.htm
- Spurgeon: they laugh at David, but God laughs at them. He sent them away empty-handed, fooled by Michal, and even the cleverest enemies of the church are ridiculous to him. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps059.php
- Guzik: their danger was real, but they were nothing against God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-59/

**v. 9**
- On the text (KJV "his strength"): Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary prefer "my strength" (O my strength, as in v. 17), following ancient versions and some manuscripts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/59.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/59.htm
- Gill and Barnes keep "his strength": Saul's strength is so great that David looks to God alone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/59.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-59.html
- Calvin (quoted by Spurgeon): Saul's strength is in God's hands and held back by his providence. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps059.cfm
- Fausset (quoted by Spurgeon): "keep watch for You" echoes the title. David's watching *for God* answers their watching *to kill him*. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps059.cfm
- Guzik: "fortress" means a high tower. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-59/

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: "will come to meet me" (KJV "prevent") means God comes to meet him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/59.htm
- Spurgeon calls this "preventing mercy," help prepared before the need arises. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps059.php
- Gill: the written Hebrew text has "his mercy," while the traditional reading is "my mercy." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/59.htm
- Guzik: it is *my* God of mercy, personal rather than distant. Meyer finds three titles in vv. 9–10: God of mercy, high tower and strength. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-59/
- "My desire" is not in the Hebrew. Spurgeon says the sense is that David will look at his enemies without fear, as Christ and Stephen looked on their killers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps059.cfm
- Utley: "look triumphantly" is a common phrase for victory. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21558

**v. 11** (the main difficulty)
- Guzik: David wanted his enemies defeated in the way that would teach God's people the most. He quotes Poole: this shows David acted for God's honour, not out of private malice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-59/
- Barnes: the point is that the lesson should last and not be quickly forgotten. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/59-11.html
- Spurgeon: enemies keep God's servants awake, so make them wanderers like Cain, living warnings. He calls it a soldier's prayer, "untempered by the gentleness of Jesus." https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps059.php
- Ellicott: "scatter" means "make them wander," the word used of Cain. He asks where else anyone wishes for drawn-out punishment for Israel's moral good. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/59.htm
- Utley compares God leaving Canaanites in the land after the conquest so Israel would grow in faith. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21558
- Utley: "our shield" goes back to God's promise to Abraham (Gen 15:1). https://bible.org/book/export/html/21558
- *Historic reading you'll need to handle with care:* Gill, Diodati (quoted by Spurgeon) and the Pulpit Commentary all apply "scatter them" to the Jewish people's dispersion after Christ was rejected. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/59-11.html ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps059.cfm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/59.htm

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: the Hebrew is hard. He renders it "by the sin of their mouth… let them be taken in their pride," meaning their slanders come back on their own heads. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/59.htm
- Pulpit gives other renderings, e.g. "O the sin of their mouth!" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/59.htm
- Spurgeon: sins of the lips are real sins that will be punished. Let them be caught in their own net. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps059.php
- Coffman: notably, the sin singled out in these murderers is their tongue. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/psalms-59.html

**v. 13**
- Guzik: this doesn't contradict v. 11. David just wanted God to deal with them however he chose. He compares David's words to Goliath (1 Sam 17:46). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-59/
- Pulpit makes the same comparison, but says David "forgets" his earlier wish. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/59.htm
- Spurgeon's notes: "that they may be no more" may mean a wretched condition rather than complete destruction. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps059.cfm
- Gill: it means the loss of their former glory, and "God rules over Jacob" refers to Christ's kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/59-13.html

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: David turns from his enemies' future back to their present state. He is still being hunted, but by morning he will be gone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/59.htm
- Guzik: the line is repeated for emphasis. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-59/

**v. 15**
- On the word "growl": Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary say it properly means "stay all night," still hoping to catch him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-59.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/59.htm
- Ellicott prefers "if not satisfied they growl," following the ancient Greek and Latin translations, Jerome and Luther. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/59.htm
- Pulpit (quoted by Coffman): "David himself was the prey." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/59-16.html
- Matthew Henry: the wicked are never satisfied, and discontent, not poverty, makes a person unhappy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/59.htm

**v. 16**
- Guzik: the dogs howl, but David sings, even though the plot is still in place. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-59/
- Barnes: the night stands for sorrow, and the morning for relief. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/59-16.html
- Matthew Henry: when the night of trouble is over, God's people sing in the morning. He adds that power without mercy is frightening, and mercy without power can't help. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/59.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/59-9.html
- Chuck Smith: leave your defence entirely to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/59-16.html

**v. 17**
- Spurgeon's notes: "my strength" answers the enemy's strength (v. 9). Calvin: God holds the strength of the wicked in check and supports his own people. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps059.cfm
- Pulpit: the verse matches v. 9 if "my strength" is read there. "God of my mercy" means the God who shows me mercy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/59.htm

**Comments on the psalm's harsh prayers as a whole (vv. 5, 11–13)**
- A note in Spurgeon: remember the different ages of God's dealings, and David's zeal for God's glory. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps059.cfm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: if there is revenge in David's wish, he is no example to us, and for Christians it would be sinful. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/59-9.html

---

**Gaps to fill if you re-run the research:**
- Lutheran, Wesleyan and Pentecostal writers
- Catholic and Orthodox readings, including Augustine's exposition on newadvent.org (the Douay numbering is Psalm 58)
- netbible.org notes
- Calvin directly, rather than through Spurgeon's quotations
